statements.claim: King Bhishmaka of Kundina had let his son (Rukmi) send out swayamvara invitations against his own wishes, and the invited kings were arriving by chariot, elephant, horse and infantry until the streets seemed full of armed men.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.108: Krishna charges that Bhishmaka must know of 'the great assemblage of the kings invited by your son', where 'cars, elephants, horses and the infantry have made a wild dance in your city'; Bhishmaka himself says his son 'wishes to give away his sister in a Swayamvara, but I do not like it'. The inviter-son (Rukmi) and swayamvara announcement rest on 1.103 ('Rukshmini, the first sister of Rukshmi, will hold her Swayamvara') continuity.

statements.claim: Bhishmaka came to Krishna saying his son out of childishness wished to give away his sister in a swayamvara, that he wanted his daughter to choose the one person she saw, and begged forgiveness for his son's bad conduct.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.108, Bhishmaka's speech near-verbatim: 'out of his childish nature, my son wishes to give away his sister in a Swayamvara, but I do not like it... I wish that my daughter may select the only person whom she sees... Be thou propitiated and forgive (him).'

statements.claim: Krishna rebuked Bhishmaka that a king who speaks a falsehood consumes himself with the fire of Yama's tortures, and that truthfulness is the foremost religious duty of kings, pointed out by Brahma in the days of yore.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.108: 'He who... speaks a falsehood, even before one king, consumes with the fire of Yama's tortures'; 'even Brahmā, in the days of yore, pointed it out as the foremost duty of men.'

statements.claim: Krishna accused Bhishmaka of pretending not to know of the gathering and of withholding hospitality from him, citing Manu's rule that he who puts obstacles in the way of a maiden wastes himself in hell; he said that was why he had not entered the assembly hall, that Kaishika had given rest to his followers, and that he lived there with Garuda as in the city of the gods.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.108: 'you have offered hospitality and welcome duly to the kings, assembled like the sun and moon... and still you do not know anything of your son's work'; 'Manu and other leading Law-givers have ordained that he who puts obstacles in the way of a maiden, wastes himself in hell'; 'for this, I did not enter into the assembly-hall and accept hospitality... Kaishika, ever fond of guests, offered us proper hospitality. I too, in the company of Garuda, am living here as in the city of gods.'

statements.claim: Bhishmaka bowed low under Krishna's words, begged forgiveness as one possessed by ignorance, asked for 'eyes of wisdom', and said that having obtained Krishna's shelter he entertained no fear.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.108 near-verbatim: 'I am possessed by the darkness of ignorance; do thou give me eyes of wisdom... Having obtained thy shelter, I do not entertain any fear.'

statements.claim: Krishna revealed that Rukmini's goddess-like form had brought him to Kundina, and that when the gods assembled on the summit of Mount Sumeru in the days of yore they told her to be born in Bhishmaka's house in Kundina and be united with Keshava.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.108: 'the goddess-like form of Rukshmini has brought me to this place'; 'When in the days of yore the gods assembled on the summit of the mount Sumeru for incarnating their portions they said to her... having been born in the house of Bhishmaka in the city of Kundina, be thou united with Keshava.'

statements.claim: Rukmini is not a woman but the goddess Lakshmi (Sree), born among mortals at the words of Brahma, and must not be given away in a swayamvara before all the kings; she should be conferred on a single invited bridegroom with proper rites, as a Kshatriya's duty.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.108: 'truly your daughter Rukshmini is not a woman; she is the very goddess Sree. For some object and at the words of Brahmā she is born (as a woman)'; 'She should not be given away in a Swayamvara where all the kings will be assembled... inviting one bride groom, you should confer her on him. It will be thus performing a Kshatriya's duties. O king, you cannot give away Lakshmi in a Swayamvara.'

statements.claim: Garuda, son of Vinata, had been sent by the king of the gods to obstruct the swayamvara, and Krishna himself had come to witness the festival of the kings and see Rukmini.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.108: 'In order to put impediments in Swayamvara Vinata's son has been despatched by the king of gods and has come to the city of Kundina. I too have come here to witness this Swayamvara festivity of the kings and your daughter, the beautiful Kamala without lotuses.'

statements.claim: Bhishmaka's anxious mood as the affair slipped from his hands, and the closing reflection that what he had feared was the will of the gods.
statements.evidence: Inner-state framing around the supported dialogue (his dislike of the swayamvara is in the passage); no new sourceable factual assertion.

notes: Dialogue tracks Harivamsha 1.108 near-verbatim (Dutt/Gutenberg #61937). Rukmi as the inviting son rests on 1.103/1.108 continuity; the pack itself does not name him in this chapter.

statements.claim: After the audience in which Krishna had told Bhishmaka of the gods' decree about Rukmini, Krishna rose to take his leave and the kings of the swayamvara were stirring in the city.
statements.evidence: Pack index summary: 'Krishna takes leave of Bhishmaka'; Harivamsha 1.109 opens 'After the departure of Vasudeva's son the kings... returned to the assembly-hall'. The decree (Rukmini as Lakshmi to be united with Keshava) is DKS_0192/1.108 continuity.

statements.claim: As he was leaving, Bhishmaka beheld Krishna's universal form: the prime and self-sprung Krishna, existing before every beginning, with eyes like red lotuses, a thousand feet, a thousand eyes and a thousand arms.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Harivamsha 1.108): 'beholding the prime and self-sprung Krishna, having eyes like red lotuses, thousand feet, thousand eyes, thousand arms'.

statements.claim: Bhishmaka bowed low and began to eulogise Krishna's glories, praising the self-sprung one as the source of everything.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (1.108): 'the king Bhishmaka bowed unto him and began to eulogise his glories'; the eulogy of the prime/self-sprung lord is the subject of the passage.

statements.claim: The vision then folded back and Krishna stood before Bhishmaka again as the young man he had seemed, ready to leave.
statements.evidence: The pack records the cosmic-form sight, the eulogy and Krishna's departure (1.109 opening: kings return to the assembly hall 'after the departure of Vasudeva's son') without detailing the reversion; the return to mortal form is the connective bridge between the two scenes.

statements.claim: As Krishna came out of Bhishmaka's presence, the assembled kings who had come to Kundina rose and followed him.
statements.evidence: Pack index summary: '...worships him with a eulogy before the kings follow him out'. The kings' motivations ('as if drawn...') are connective gloss.

statements.claim: The 'young man who had claimed her' gloss in the closing lines, Bhishmaka's inner awe, and cosmic-form elaboration ('the shape of everything, every being that breathed, every star').
statements.evidence: Atmosphere elaborating the pack's epithets (prime, self-sprung, thousand-limbed); 'claimed her' gestures to the gods' decree of DKS_0192 rather than asserting a new event.

notes: Core scene matches 1.108-1.109 pack: leave-taking, cosmic form with thousand feet/eyes/arms, eulogy, kings following him out. Story uses 'thousand feet/eyes/arms' matching the excerpt (the index summary's 'thousand heads and arms' is the loose variant; the excerpt governs). Poetic expansion is atmosphere.

statements.claim: After Krishna left Kundina, the kings who had come for the swayamvara gathered one last time in Bhishmaka's assembly hall, anxious to be on the road to their own kingdoms.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.109.1: 'After the departure of Vasudeva's son the kings, who... were anxious to go to their respective kingdoms, returned to the assembly-hall of Bhishmaka.'

statements.claim: Bhishmaka, foremost of kings and well-read in the moral laws, asked the assembled kings' forgiveness for the calamity and for the fruit of his misconduct.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.109.2-3 near-verbatim: 'the foremost of kings and well-read in moral laws... O ye kings, you all know the calamity that will befall the Swayamvara. Do you forgive me for the fruit that is the outcome of my misconduct.'

statements.claim: He honored the kings and sent them on their way — the monarchs of central India and of the east, west and north — and they, mighty car-warriors, returned his honors and rode off delighted.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.109.4-5: 'the king sent away all the monarchs of Central India and of the East, West and Northern Provinces. Having honored the king Bhishmaka duly in return, those kings, the foremost of men and mighty car-warriors, went away delightedly.'

statements.claim: A few kings remained with Bhishmaka — Jarasandha, Sunitha, Dantavakra, the king of Soubha and others of the Deccan — lingering as if sensing the mystery of Kundina was unfinished.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.109.5-6: 'Jarāsandha, Sunitha, the energetic Dantavakra, the king of Soubha... all those and other kings of the Deccan remained by Bhishmaka desirous of listening to the mystery.'

statements.claim: Rukmini had seen Krishna, had heard him speak, and had watched her father's fear drain away in his presence.
statements.evidence: The pack (Harivamsha 1.109) places Rukmini's declaration among her friends after the kings' dispersal and nowhere shows her at Krishna's audience with Bhishmaka (1.108), which the preceding corpus stories present as private. The Bhagavata branch of this same abduction cluster (10.52, cf. DKS_0196-97) has her choose Krishna purely by hearsay — her own message opens 'Having heard your virtues' (10.52.36) — and DKS_0196 states she settled her marriage 'without ever having set eyes on the groom.'

statements.claim: Everything her brother Rukmi had planned — the invitations, the gathering of kings, the ceremony where she would choose — was swayamvara machinery built on treating her as a prize.
statements.evidence: Corpus continuity of the pack's own chain: 1.103 spies announce Rukmini's swayamvara; 1.108 has Krishna speak of 'the great assemblage of the kings invited by your son'; a swayamvara is by definition a public choosing-ceremony.

statements.claim: Rukmini approached her friends with her face bent down in shame and declared she would not be the spouse of anyone save Krishna, who has lotus eyes.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Harivamsha 1.109) near-verbatim: 'the chaste and wise Rukshmini approached her friends and with her face bent down in shame said:—I tell you truly, I do not wish to be the spouse of any body else save Krishna having lotus eyes.'

statements.claim: Rukmini's shyness as burning confession, the certainty of her secret choice, and the reflection that no assembly can overrule a bride who has decided.
statements.evidence: Inner-state and thematic narration around the supported declaration; no new sourceable factual assertion.

corrections.original_sentence: Rukmini had seen Krishna. She had heard him speak, and she had watched her father's fear drain away in his presence.
corrections.suggested: Rukmini had never set eyes on Krishna; she knew him only through the reports of his beauty and virtues that had reached Kundina, and her heart had already answered them.

notes: Assembly, dismissal, the kings who stayed, and Rukmini's declaration all track Harivamsha 1.109 closely. One unsupported embellishment: Rukmini personally witnessing Krishna's audience with her father — no pack support, and the sibling BhP branch (10.52) plus DKS_0196 say she chose him by hearing alone.

statements.claim: Years later Uddhava, who had served Krishna, remembered two of Krishna's weddings together: Rukmini's carrying off and Satya (Nagnajiti)'s svayamvara victory.
statements.evidence: Pack title/summary (BhP 3.3): 'Uddhava recalls how Krishna carried off Rukmini, Bhishmaka's daughter, by the gandharva rite, and how he defeated the proud kings to win Satya (Nagnajiti) at her svayamvara'; variant_notes: 'Recall bundling Rukmini's abduction + Satya's svayamvara.'

statements.claim: Rukmini, Bhishmaka's daughter, sent for Krishna, and he came and carried off his own share by the gandharva rite while the assembled suitors looked on.
statements.evidence: BhP 3.3.2: 'samāhutā bhīṣmaka-kanyayā' (summoned by Bhishmaka's daughter); pack excerpt: 'he carried off his own share by the gandharva rite while the suitors looked on.'

statements.claim: Rukmini had already chosen Krishna, her choice known only to her and the man she had called, so Krishna came as a bridegroom answering a bride, not as a suitor entering a contest.
statements.evidence: The summons of 3.3.2 implies the prior secret choice, established in the cluster (DKS_0194 declaration among friends; DKS_0196-97 secret message). The 'his own share' phrasing of the pack verse confirms the pre-ordained match.

statements.claim: A gandharva marriage is the old rite in which a man and woman take each other by consent alone, without priest, fire or assembly.
statements.evidence: Explanatory gloss of the rite named in the source (3.3.2 'gandharva rite'); standard meaning, not a pack-cited fact.

statements.claim: The swayamvara ended without a garland being placed; Krishna claimed his destined bride openly before the whole gathering of suitors, and the competition was over before it began.
statements.evidence: 3.3.2: he 'carried off his own share by the gandharva rite while the suitors looked on' — the onlooking suitors are spectators, not competitors; 'his share / bride the gods had destined' echoes the gods' decree (1.108, DKS_0192).

statements.claim: Satya, the princess called Nagnajiti, held her svayamvara in her own kingdom, where no summons or secret message preceded Krishna's coming and the proudest kings vied for her.
statements.evidence: BhP 3.3.3: 'svayaṃvare nāgnajitīm uvāha' — he took Nagnajiti at her svayamvara; the absence of any summons contrasts with verse 2's 'samāhutā bhīṣmaka-kanyayā' (Rukmini summoned him).

statements.claim: At Satya's svayamvara Krishna met the proud kings, humbled and defeated them, and Satya went with him as his bride.
statements.evidence: BhP 3.3.3: 'kakudmino 'viddha-naso damitvā' (subduing the unbridled bull-like/proud kings); pack excerpt: 'humbling the proud kings, he won Nagnajiti at her svayamvara.'

statements.claim: Framing: Uddhava remembered this years afterward in the palace at Dwaraka, with Rukmini and Satya, the two brides of his Lord, ruling that great house beside him.
statements.evidence: Uddhava-POV framing device; the pack (two verses) does not locate the recollection. BhP 3.3's canonical setting is Uddhava's later narration, so the Dwaraka-palace vignette is connective frame rather than an asserted source fact.

notes: Core content matches BhP 3.3.2-3 closely (Rukmini summoned and carried off by the gandharva rite; Satya/Nagnajiti won by humbling the kings at her svayamvara). The Uddhava-recollection frame and rite gloss are connective; the story's own tradition_note flags this as the condensed Bhagavata recall.

statements.claim: Rukmini, daughter of Bhishmaka, king of Kundina in Vidarbha, settled her own marriage by report — having heard of Krishna's beauty and virtues — before she ever set eyes on the groom.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.22: 'sopaśrutya mukundasya rūpa-vīrya-guṇa-śriyaḥ' (she heard of Mukunda's beauty, might, qualities and glory); pack excerpt: 'heard of Krishna's beauty and virtues and resolved he alone was a fitting husband'; the Vaidarbhī epithet (10.52.25) supports 'princess of Vidarbha'.

statements.claim: Her brother Rukmi had decided her future: he meant to give her to Shishupala, and the household moved toward the wedding as toward something already decided.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (BhP 10.52.14-27 rendering): 'though her brother Rukmi wished to give her to Shishupala'; 10.52.21 lists Rukmi as her foremost brother ('rukmy agrajo').

statements.claim: Word of Krishna of Dwaraka reached Kundina through travelers and brahmanas, and the more she heard the more she was convinced he alone was a fitting husband.
statements.evidence: 10.52.22 (śrutvā — by hearing) and the pack excerpt: 'heard of Krishna's beauty and virtues and resolved he alone was a fitting husband'.

statements.claim: Knowing her brother would not listen, Rukmini kept her wish from her family, found a brahmana she trusted completely, and sent him out swiftly and in secret to Dwaraka with a message for Krishna alone.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'she sent a trusted brahmana swiftly to Dwaraka'; 10.52.25-26 have her distressed (durmanā) and the brahmana reaching Dwaraka; secrecy and single addressee follow from the message account (10.52.28-42, DKS_0197) and her brother's opposed plan.

statements.claim: The brahmana took the long road from Vidarbha to Dwaraka and was admitted past the city's guards and brought to Krishna's presence.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.26: 'dvārakāṃ sa samabhyetya pratīhāraiḥ praveśitaḥ' (coming to Dwaraka he was admitted by the gatekeepers).

statements.claim: When Krishna saw the travel-worn brahmana he rose from his own seat and received him as a guest of the first rank, for he held brahmanas in the highest honor.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.27: 'dṛṣṭvā brahmaṇya-devas tam avaruhya nijāsanāt' (seeing him, the Lord devoted to brahmanas descended from his own seat) — the brahmaṇya-deva epithet grounds the 'highest honor for brahmanas' clause.

statements.claim: The court watched the welcome, the two spoke quietly together, and Rukmini's message passed out of the messenger's keeping into Krishna's.
statements.evidence: Bridge narration to the message itself (10.52.28-42), which is the subject of the following story (DKS_0197); no new factual assertion.

notes: Faithful to BhP 10.52.14-27: hearing-based choice (śrutvā guṇān), the Rukmi-Shishupala plan, the trusted brahmana sent to Dwaraka, and Krishna rising for the brahmana. The 'never set eyes on the groom' framing is consistent with the pack's hearing-based account.

statements.claim: Krishna asked after the messenger before the message: whether his dharma was still approved by elders, whether as a brahmana he was content with whatever came by chance (for an unsatisfied man, even a lord of the gods, wanders from world to world), after the brahmanas of Vidarbha, and how he had crossed the difficult road.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.28-34: 'kaccid dvija-vara-śreṣṭha dharmas te vṛddha-sammataḥ'; 'asantuṣṭo 'sakṛl lokān āpnoty api sureśvaraḥ'; 'viprān sva-lābha-santuṣṭān sādhūn bhūta-suhṛttamān'; 'yatas tvam āgato durgaṃ nistīryeha'.

statements.claim: Rukmini's message opened: 'Having heard your virtues, O beauty of the three worlds, my heart has entered into you, and it is not ashamed'; your virtues entering through the ear take away the body's distress, and your form is the whole reward of a seeing eye.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.36: 'śrutvā guṇān bhuvana-sundara... tvayy acyutāviśati cittam apatrapaṃ me'; 'nirviśya karṇa-vivarair harato 'ṅga-tāpam'; 'rūpaṃ dṛśāṃ dṛśimatām akhilārtha-lābham'.

statements.claim: The message asked what wise girl of a good family would not choose him — one without equal in family, conduct, beauty, learning, youth and wealth, who delights the minds of men.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.37: 'kā... mahatī kula-śīla-rūpa-vidyā-vayo-draviṇa-dhāmabhir ātma-tulyam dhīrā patiṃ kulavatī na vṛṇīta kanyā... nara-loka-mano-'bhirāmam'.

statements.claim: 'You are the one I have chosen. I have given myself to you.'
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.38: 'tan me bhavān khalu vṛtaḥ patir aṅga jāyām / ātmārpitaś ca bhavato 'tra vibho vidhehi'.

statements.claim: 'Do not let the king of Cedi touch the hero's share — do not let Shishupala, like a jackal, seize the lion's prey.'
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.38: 'mā vīra-bhāgam abhimarśatu caidya ārād / gomāyu-van mṛga-pater balim ambujākṣa' (let not the Caidya from afar touch the hero's share, like a jackal the lion's prey, O lotus-eyed one).

statements.claim: If the Lord, worshipped with sacrifices, gifts and vows and honored in gods, brahmanas and elders, is pleased with her devotion, let him come and take her hand — not Damaghosha's son, not any other.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.39: 'pūrteṣṭa-datta-niyama-vrata-deva-vipra-gurv-arcanādibhir alaṃ bhagavān pareśaḥ / ārādhito yadi gadāgraja etya pāṇiṃ gṛhṇātu me na damaghoṣa-sutādayo 'nye'.

statements.claim: The message said 'Tomorrow they will marry me': Krishna should come to Vidarbha in secret surrounded by his warriors, crush the forces of the king of Cedi and the king of Magadha, and carry her off by the rakshasa rite as the prize of his valour.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.40: 'śvo bhāvini tvam ajitodvahane vidarbhān guptaḥ sametya pṛtanā-patibhiḥ parītaḥ / nirmathya caidya-magadhendra-balaṃ prasahya māṃ rākṣasena vidhinodvaha vīrya-śulkām'.

statements.claim: She told him how: she lived within the inner apartments, so her kinsmen could not be killed — on the day before the wedding there is a great procession of the family goddess, in which the new bride goes out to the temple of Girija.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.41: 'antaḥ-purāntara-carīm anihatya bandhūn tvām udvahe katham iti pravadāmy upāyam / pūrve-dyur asti mahatī kula-deva-yātrā yasyāṃ bahir nava-vadhūr girijām upeyāt'.

statements.claim: The message closed: if she did not obtain his grace she would give up this body, weakened by her vows, and even a hundred births would not change her choice.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.52.42: 'yarhy ambujākṣa na labheya bhavat-prasādaṃ jahyām asūn vrata-kṛśān śata-janmabhiḥ syāt'.

notes: Rukmini's message is rendered nearly verse-by-verse from BhP 10.52.28-42 (GRETIL), including the pre-message dialogue (10.52.28-35) and the rakshasa-rite / Girija-procession plan. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Krishna heard the brahmana out and said, 'I too cannot sleep at night for her sake,' declaring he would bring her back, crushing in battle the wicked kings who stood in his way.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.2-3 ('śrī-bhagavān uvāca / tām ānayiṣya unmathya rājanyāpasadān mṛdhe') and pack excerpt: 'Krishna said "I too cannot sleep at night for her"'.

statements.claim: No council was called and no army mustered; the chariot was made ready with the four horses Shaibya, Sugriva, Meghapushpa and Balahaka, Krishna seated the brahmana beside him, and Daruka his charioteer took the reins.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.4-5: 'sa cāśvaiḥ śaibya-sugrīva-meghapuṣpa-balāhakaiḥ... āruhya syandanaṃ śaurir dvijam āropya'; Daruka is named among the pack's own character list for this event and is Krishna's standing charioteer.

statements.claim: Krishna crossed the Dwaraka-Kundina road in a single night, and by sunrise he was within the borders of Vidarbha.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (BhP 10.53.1-20 rendering): 'he set out at once and reached Vidarbha in a single night'.

statements.claim: In Kundina, Bhishmaka — led by love for his son — had the streets swept and sprinkled, the roads and crossings cleaned, and garlands, perfumes and bright garments readied; he worshipped the ancestors, gods and brahmanas according to the rites; the bride was bathed and adorned with the auspicious ceremonies, foremost brahmanas chanted Sama, Rig and Yajur mantras over her for protection, and gifts of gold, silver, garments and sesame mixed with jaggery were distributed.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.6-12 near-verbatim: 'rājā sa kuṇḍina-patiḥ putra-sneha-vaśānugaḥ'; 'puraṃ sammṛṣṭa-saṃsikta-mārga-rathyā-catuṣpatham'; 'pitṝn devān samabhyarcya viprāṃś ca vidhi-vat'; 'su-snātāṃ... kṛta-kautuka-maṅgalām'; 'cakruḥ sāma-rg-yajur-mantrair vadhvā rakṣāṃ dvijottamāḥ'; 'hiraṇya-rūpya vāsāṃsi tilāṃś ca guḍa-miśritān'.

statements.claim: Damaghosha, the king of Cedi, came for his son with herds of rutting elephants and chariots garlanded with gold, and the lord of Vidarbha went out to receive him with honor.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.13-15: 'cedi-patī rājā damaghoṣaḥ sutāya vai / mada-cyudbhir gajānīkaiḥ syandanair hema-mālibhiḥ / taṃ vai vidarbhādhipatiḥ samabhyetyābhipūjya ca'.

statements.claim: With Damaghosha came Shalva, Jarasandha of Magadha, Dantavakra and Viduratha — kings who hated Krishna and Balarama and were determined to give the bride to the prince of Cedi, resolving 'If Krishna comes, we will fight him together.'
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.16-18: 'tatra śālvo jarāsandho dantavakro vidūrathaḥ / kṛṣṇa-rāma-dviṣo yattāḥ kanyāṃ caidyāya sādhitum / yotsyāmaḥ saṃhatās tena iti niścita-mānasāḥ'. Jarasandha's Magadha kingship is established corpus continuity (DKS_0189).

statements.claim: Word of the muster reached Balarama, who — flooded with love for his brother — gathered a great force and set out after him.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.19-20: 'śrutvaitad bhagavān rāmo vipakṣīya nṛpodyamam / balena mahatā sārdhaṃ bhrātṛ-sneha-pariplutaḥ'.

statements.claim: Rukmini, in the inner apartments, counted the hours toward a wedding she had never wanted, hoping the man she had written to had heard her message in time.
statements.evidence: Core is supported by 10.53.21-22 ('bhīṣma-kanyā... kāṅkṣanty āgamanaṃ hareḥ'; 'tri-yāmāntarita udvāho me'); the emotional gloss is connective narration.

notes: Scene-by-scene match with BhP 10.53.1-20: Krishna's sleepless resolve, the four named horses, the overnight journey, Kundina's wedding preparations, Damaghosha's arrival, the hostile kings' pact, and Balarama's pursuit. Daruka is in the pack's character list and is Krishna's standing charioteer.

statements.claim: With a single night left before her wedding and Krishna not yet arrived, Rukmini's mind, stolen by Govinda, would not rest: 'Will the faultless one find something blameworthy in me? The creator is not favorable to me, nor Maheshvara' — and tears came as she prayed that Krishna alone might be her husband.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.21-25: 'kāṅkṣanty āgamanaṃ hareḥ'; 'tri-yāmāntarita udvāho me 'lpa-rādhasaḥ'; 'api mayy anavadyātmā dṛṣṭvā kiñcij jugupsitam'; 'durbhagāyā na me dhātā nānukūlo maheśvaraḥ'; 'evaṃ cintayatī bālā govinda-hṛta-mānasā'.

statements.claim: The same brahmana she had sent to Dwaraka returned, sent back now by Krishna himself, with a bright face and news that lifted her heart: the darling of the Yadus had reached Vidarbha.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.27-29: 'atha kṛṣṇa-vinirdiṣṭaḥ sa eva dvija-sattamaḥ'; 'sā taṃ prahṛṣṭa-vadanam...'; 'tasyā āvedayat prāptaṃ śaśaṃsa yadu-nandanam'.

statements.claim: Bhishmaka, hearing Krishna had arrived among the gathered kings, offered the madhuparka — the honeyed welcome — with fresh garments and had a splendid residence made ready for him.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.31-33: 'madhu-parkam upānīya vāsāṃsi virajāṃsi saḥ / tayor niveśanaṃ śrīmad upākalpya mahā-matiḥ'. The Sanskrit dual (tayor) reflects both arrivals (Krishna and Balarama, who follows per 10.53.19-20 / DKS_0198); the story's singular is compression, not contradiction.

statements.claim: The townspeople of Vidarbha said openly: 'Rukmini deserves to be his wife, and no other. What good deed did we do, that the maker of the three worlds should be pleased with us?' — and love bound the whole city.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.35-38 near-verbatim: 'kṛṣṇam āgatam ākarṇya vidarbha-pura-vāsinaḥ / asyaiva bhāryā bhavituṃ rukmiṇy arhati nāparā / kiñcit su-caritaṃ yan nas tena tuṣṭas tri-loka-kṛt / evaṃ prema-kalā-baddhā vadanti sma puraukasaḥ'.

statements.claim: On the day of the family goddess's procession — the day her message had pointed to — Rukmini, wrapped in a vow of silence, went out on foot with her mothers and companions to see the lotus-petal feet of Bhavani, while thousands of women followed with offerings and singers and musicians played.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.39-42: 'padbhyāṃ viniryayau draṣṭuṃ bhavānyāḥ pāda-pallavam / yata-vāṅ mātṛbhiḥ sārdhaṃ sakhībhiḥ parivāritā / nānopahāra balibhir vāramukhyāḥ sahasraśaḥ / gāyantyaś ca stuvantaś ca gāyakā vādya-vādakāḥ'.

statements.claim: At the shrine Rukmini washed her hands and feet; the elderly brahmana women versed in the rites worshipped the goddess with water, perfume, unbroken rice, incense, fresh garments, garlands and ornaments, joined by the married women of the household, who then gave Rukmini the remainder of the offerings and pronounced blessings over her.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.43-48: 'āsādya devī-sadanaṃ dhauta-pāda-karāmbujā'; 'pravayaso... vidhi-jñā vipra-yoṣitaḥ'; 'adbhir gandhākṣatair dhūpair vāsaḥ-sraṅ-mālya bhūṣaṇaiḥ'; 'vipra-striyaḥ patimatīs tathā taiḥ samapūjayat'; 'tasyai striyas tāḥ pradaduḥ śeṣāṃ yuyujur āśiṣaḥ'.

statements.claim: Bowing before the goddess, Rukmini prayed the one prayer she had carried in her heart: may Krishna, the Lord, alone become my husband — 'bless this.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (BhP 10.53.20-52): 'she bowed: May Krishna, the Lord, alone become my husband; bless this.'

statements.claim: She rose, laid aside her vow of silence, and came out of Ambika's temple; the assembled heroes who saw her — slim-waisted, her face bright with earrings, her smile pure, her lips like bimba fruit, her teeth like jasmine buds — stood struck with love.
statements.evidence: BhP 10.53.49-52 near-verbatim: 'muni-vratam atha tyaktvā niścakrāmāmbikā-gṛhāt / tāṃ deva-māyām iva... su-madhyamāṃ kuṇḍala-maṇḍitānanām / śuci-smitāṃ bimba-phalādhara-dyuti-śoṇāyamāna-dvija-kunda-kuḍmalām / vilokya vīrā mumuhuḥ samāgatā yaśasvinas tat-kṛta-hṛc-chayārditāḥ'.

statements.claim: 'Only one man in all that crowd did not stare. Krishna had come, as she had asked him to' — and the procession that was to deliver her to Shishupala would deliver her to Krishna instead.
statements.evidence: Krishna's presence at the abduction scene is the immediate sequel of this event (10.54; DKS_0200 next in chain), and the 'assembled heroes' of v.52 set the scene; the 'only one man did not stare' beat is connective colour.

notes: Very close rendering of BhP 10.53.20-52: Rukmini's one-night anxiety, the messenger's return, Bhishmaka's madhuparka, the townsfolk's words, the Bhavani/Ambika procession and worship, her prayer, and the heroes' enchantment. Ambika/Bhavani/Girija are used interchangeably as in the source.
